AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug). 'The fifth day after' 7 Artemisius ≈ 12 Iyar (11–12 depending on counting); recaptured about four days later.

t: Banks against the Antonia built 12–29 Artemisius, then burned
n: John of Gischala tunnelled under the banks and set the props alight, and Simon's men burned the other engines. Josephus: "“the Romans began to raise their banks on the twelfth day of the month Artemisius, [Jyar,] so had they much ado to finish them by the twenty-ninth day”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug). The banks were begun 12 Iyar and finished on the 29th (this date); they were destroyed in the days after.

t: Titus builds a wall around the city in three days
n: The wall, 39 furlongs with 13 forts, sealed the city and the famine became extreme. Josephus: "“the whole was completed in three days”". After the banks were lost (end of Iyar), so early Daesius/Sivan AD 70.

t: 115,880 dead carried out through a single gate
n: Mannaeus son of Lazarus reported the count to Titus; deserters said 600,000 poor had been thrown out of the gates. Josephus: "“between the fourteenth day of the month Xanthieus, [Nisan,] when the Romans pitched their camp by the city, and the first day of the month Panemus [Tamuz]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug). The figure covers 14 Nisan to 1 Tammuz; it is dated here at the end of the count.

t: Attack on the Antonia; the undermined wall collapses
n: A Jewish sally against the banks failed. That night John's mine brought the Antonia wall down, but a new inner wall stood behind it. Josephus: "“This attack was made upon the first day of the month Panemus [Tamuz.]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

t: Captured deserters crucified, up to 500 a day
n: Josephus says 'room was wanting for the crosses, and crosses wanting for the bodies'. Josephus: "“they caught every day five hundred Jews; nay, some days they caught more”".

t: Simon bar Giora executes the high priest Matthias and his sons
n: The man who had let Simon in was killed in sight of the Romans with three sons, accused of favouring them. Josephus: "Simon “would not suffer Matthias, by whose means he got possession of the city, to go off without torment”".

t: The Syrian soldier Sabinus dies scaling the Antonia wall
n: Sabinus led eleven men up the new wall and was killed. Josephus: "“These things were done upon the third day of the month Panemus [Tamuz]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

t: Famine: Mary of Bethezob eats her own child
n: Josephus tells it as the worst horror of the famine, recalling the curses of Deuteronomy 28:56–57. It hardened Titus's resolve. Josephus: "“There was a certain woman that dwelt beyond Jordan, her name was Mary”".

t: Jesus son of Ananus killed by a siege stone, still crying “Woe”
n: On the wall he cried 'Woe to me also' and was killed by a stone from a Roman engine. Josephus: "after “seven years and five months”: “Woe, woe to myself also!”".

t: John of Gischala gives himself up from the tunnels
n: John, starved out, surrendered and was sentenced to life imprisonment; 2,000 dead were found in the tunnels. Josephus: "“As for John, he wanted food, together with his brethren, in these caverns, and begged that the Romans would now give him their right hand”; “John condemned to perpetual imprisonment”".

t: Simon bar Giora rises from the ground in white and purple on the Temple site
n: After failing to tunnel out, Simon tried to frighten the guards. He was chained and kept for the triumph. Josephus: "Simon “put on a white frock… and appeared out of the ground in the place where the temple had formerly been”".

t: Antioch: the apostate Antiochus accuses the Jews and the Sabbath is suppressed
n: A renegade Jew accused his people of plotting to burn the city, which led to killings and a ban on Sabbath rest. After a real fire (AD 70/71) Titus refused to expel the Jews. Josephus: "Antiochus was “not permitting them to rest on the seventh day”".

t: Romans take the Antonia by night
n: Twelve men crept up, killed the sleeping guards and sounded a trumpet. The garrison fled and the Romans fought into the Temple court until driven back. Josephus: "“two days afterward… about the ninth hour of the night, through the ruins, to the tower of Antonia”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug). 'Two days after' 3 Panemus ≈ 5 Tammuz, during the night (ninth hour).

t: Daily sacrifice ceases on 17 Panemus
n: The daily sacrifice stopped for lack of men to offer it, and Titus sent Josephus to plead with John. Rabbinic tradition (m. Taanit 4:6) also puts its end on 17 Tammuz, the fast day. Josephus: "“on that very day, which was the seventeenth day of Panemus, [Tamuz,] the sacrifice called the Daily Sacrifice had failed”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

t: Temple cloisters by the Antonia set on fire
n: The Jews burned the cloister joining the Antonia, which Josephus calls the beginning of the burning of the sanctuary; the Romans burned the next cloister on the 24th. Josephus: "“they set the north-west cloister… on fire… two days after which, or on the twenty-fourth day of the forenamed month, the Romans set fire to the cloister that joined to the other”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug). Jews' fire ≈ 22 Tammuz; Roman fire 24 Tammuz (≈ 22 Jul 70).

t: Jews trap Roman soldiers in the burning western cloister
n: The defenders filled the roof of the western cloister with wood, bitumen and pitch and pretended to retreat. Many Romans who climbed it died in the fire. Josephus: "“on the twenty-seventh day of the forenamed month [Panemus or Tamuz] contrived such a stratagem”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

t: Roman standards set up in the Temple court; Titus hailed imperator
n: The legions sacrificed to their standards in the Temple court. Loot was so plentiful that gold sold in Syria at half its value. Josephus: "“brought their ensigns to the temple and set them over against its eastern gate; and there did they offer sacrifices to them”". Immediately after the Temple burned (10 Lous), Av AD 70.

t: Titus parleys with Simon and John at the Xystus bridge
n: The tyrants asked to leave with their families for the desert. Titus refused and ordered the city burned and plundered. Josephus: "“he placed himself on the western side of the outer [court of the] temple… above the Xystus”". Av AD 70, shortly after the Temple fell.

t: Lower city burned as far as Siloam
n: The archives, the council house and the Ophel quarter were burned; the rebels held only the upper city. Josephus: "“the Romans drove the robbers out of the lower city, and set all on fire as far as Siloam”". Av AD 70.

t: Priests hand over Temple treasures to Titus
n: Jesus son of Thebuthi gave up two candlesticks, tables, bowls and the priestly vestments; the treasurer Phineas surrendered the priests' garments and spices. Josephus: "“one of the priests, the son of Thebuthus, whose name was Jesus”". Between 20 Lous and 7 Gorpiaeus AD 70.

t: Second Temple burned by the Romans
n: Titus's army burned the Temple on the Ninth of Av, fulfilling Jesus' word that not one stone would be left on another (Matt. 24:2). The day follows Ken Johnson's Ninth-of-Av table (4 August); Josephus gives the 10th of Lous, usually reckoned 30 August (Julian).
s: Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-8; Ken Johnson, Ancient Prophecies Revealed (Ninth of Av)

t: Banks completed against the Temple; Titus orders the gates set on fire
n: The rams failed against the Temple walls, so the gates were burned. The next day Titus's council argued over whether to spare the sanctuary. Josephus: "“two of the legions had completed their banks on the eighth day of the month Lous [Ab]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

t: Titus begins banks against the upper city
n: Timber had to be brought from 100 furlongs away. The Idumaeans tried to negotiate a surrender. Josephus: "“this on the twentieth day of the month Lous [Ab]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

t: Josephus's totals: 97,000 captives and 1,100,000 dead
n: He explains the numbers by the Passover crowds. A census by paschal lambs under Cestius had counted 256,500 sacrifices, about 2.7 million people. Josephus: "“the number of those that were carried captive during this whole war was… ninety-seven thousand… those that perished during the whole siege eleven hundred thousand”". Summary given after the fall (Gorpiaeus/Elul AD 70).

t: Titus orders the city and Temple razed; three towers and the west wall left
n: The rest was levelled so that visitors would not believe it had been inhabited. The 10th Legion stayed as the garrison. Josephus: "“Caesar gave orders that they should now demolish the entire city and temple, but… leave… Phasaelus, and Hippicus, and Mariamne”". Right after the capture, Gorpiaeus/Elul AD 70.

t: Banks finished and the upper city wall breached
n: The rebels lost heart, left the towers of Hippicus, Phasael and Mariamne, and fled into the valley under Siloam and the tunnels. Josephus: "“now were the banks finished on the seventh day of the month Gorpieus, [Elul,] in eighteen days' time”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

t: Jerusalem taken on 8 Gorpiaeus
n: The whole city was taken and burned. Josephus says it had been taken five times before and desolated twice, 2,177 years after its founding by Melchizedek and 1,179 years after David. Josephus: "“thus was Jerusalem taken, in the second year of the reign of Vespasian, on the eighth day of the month Gorpeius [Elul]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

t: Titus marks Domitian's birthday at Caesarea; 2,500 captives killed
n: Captives were killed fighting beasts, burned and made to fight each other. Josephus: "“he solemnized the birthday of his brother Domitian after a splendid manner”". Josephus gives no date. Domitian's birthday was 24 October (Suetonius), so 24 Oct 70.

t: Titus marks Vespasian's birthday at Berytus with more captive deaths
n: There were more shows and many more captives died. Josephus: "“exhibited a still more pompous solemnity about his father's birthday”". Josephus gives no date. Vespasian's birthday was 17 November (Suetonius), so 17 Nov 70.

t: Total solar eclipse described by Plutarch
n: Plutarch's description of a total eclipse that began near noon, with stars visible, is usually matched to this one.

t: Triumph of Vespasian and Titus in Rome; Simon bar Giora executed
n: The Temple spoils were carried, including the golden table, the lampstand and a copy of the Law. Simon was dragged to the Forum and executed. Josephus: "the procession ending “at the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus”".

t: Temple tax diverted to Jupiter Capitolinus; veterans settled at Emmaus
n: Vespasian kept Judea as his own property, settled 800 veterans at Emmaus (Motza), and imposed the Jewish tax (fiscus Judaicus). Josephus: "“enjoined every one of them to bring two drachmae every year into the Capitol”".

t: Lucilius Bassus takes Herodium
n: This began the mopping-up of the last rebel strongholds. Josephus: "Bassus “took that citadel which was in Herodium”".

t: Vespasian gives Josephus his house, citizenship and a pension
n: Josephus lived in Vespasian's old house and received lands in Judea; he wrote his histories there. Josephus: "'when we were come to Rome ... he gave me an apartment in his own house ... honored me with the privilege of a Roman citizen'".

t: Machaerus surrenders to save the young Eleazar from crucifixion
n: After the captured Eleazar was scourged and a cross set up in sight of the walls, the garrison gave up the fortress in exchange for his life. The Romans then killed the 'strangers' in the lower town. Josephus: "Bassus “resolved to besiege it, by filling up the valley that lay on the east side”".

t: Bassus destroys 3,000 fugitives in the forest of Jardes
n: Fugitives from Jerusalem and Machaerus were surrounded and killed, including Judas son of Ari. Josephus: "“he marched hastily to the forest of Jarden, as it is called”".

t: Antiochus IV of Commagene deposed (fourth year of Vespasian)
n: Caesennius Paetus accused him of plotting with Parthia; his kingdom was annexed. Josephus: "“in the fourth year of the reign of Vespasian”".

t: The Alans invade Media and Armenia
n: The Alans came through the Caspian Gates, plundered Media and nearly lassoed King Tiridates of Armenia. Josephus: "“This nation about this time laid a design of falling upon Media”".

t: Flavius Silva besieges Masada
n: Silva walled Masada round and built a ramp on the White Promontory against Eleazar son of Jair's Sicarii. Josephus: "“Flavius Silva succeeded him as procurator… made an expedition against it”".

t: Masada falls: 960 die by their own hands, 15 Xanthicus
n: After Eleazar's speeches the defenders killed their families and then each other, and burned everything but the food. Two women and five children hid and survived. Josephus: "“This calamitous slaughter was made on the fifteenth day of the month Xanthicus [Nisan]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. The year is disputed: AD 73 is traditional, AD 74 is favoured by many since inscriptions show Silva governing into 73/74. AD 74 gives ≈ 1 Apr 74 on this reckoning; other calendar readings (e.g. Tyrian) put it some weeks later.

t: Sicarii fugitives in Alexandria handed over; they refuse to call Caesar lord
n: The Jewish elders handed over 600 Sicarii. Under torture none would call Caesar lord, which Josephus admired. Josephus: "“not one of these children was so far overcome by these torments, as to name Caesar for their lord”".

t: Vespasian has the temple of Onias in Egypt closed
n: Lupus and then Paulinus took the offerings, shut the gates and stopped all worship there. Josephus: "“the duration of the time from the building of this temple till it was shut up again was three hundred and forty-three years”".

t: Jonathan the weaver leads a desert movement in Cyrene
n: Jonathan promised signs in the desert, and the governor Catullus crushed them. Catullus then killed 3,000 wealthy Jews, and Jonathan falsely accused Josephus in Rome. Josephus: "“one Jonathan, a vile person, and by trade a weaver”".

t: Vespasian's Temple of Peace receives the Temple's gold vessels
n: The Law and the purple veils of the sanctuary were kept in the palace. Josephus: "“he also laid up therein those golden vessels and instruments that were taken out of the Jewish temple”".

t: Josephus presents the Jewish War to Vespasian and Titus
n: Agrippa II wrote 62 letters vouching for it; Titus ordered it published. Josephus: "'Titus was so desirous that the knowledge of these affairs should be taken from these books alone, that he subscribed his own hand to them'".

t: Death of Vespasian
n: The emperor who began the Colosseum died, and his son Titus, who had destroyed Jerusalem, succeeded him.

t: Death of Titus
n: Titus died after a short reign marked by the eruption of Vesuvius; his brother Domitian took the throne.

t: Josephus writes about Jesus in the Antiquities (Testimonium Flavianum)
n: Josephus calls Jesus a wise man and doer of wonderful works, condemned by Pilate at the urging of leading men, and says 'the tribe of Christians, so named from him, are not extinct at this day'. Josephus: "'Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man ... Pilate ... had condemned him to the cross'".

t: Josephus completes the Antiquities in Domitian's 13th year
n: Twenty books of Jewish history from Creation to the eve of the war; the Life was added as an appendix. Josephus: "'which is the thirteenth year of the reign of Caesar Domitian, and the fifty-sixth year of my own life'".

t: Against Apion names 22 sacred books, prophecy ending with Artaxerxes
n: Five books of Moses, thirteen of the prophets and four of hymns and precepts; books after Artaxerxes were not trusted equally because 'there hath not been an exact succession of prophets'. The earliest Jewish list of the canon. Josephus: "'only twenty-two books, which contain the records of all the past times'".

t: Domitian assassinated; Nerva becomes emperor
n: Court officials murdered Domitian, whose reign Christian tradition remembers for persecution, and the Senate chose Nerva.

t: Death of Nerva; Trajan succeeds
n: Nerva died after adopting Trajan, the first emperor from the provinces.

t: Hadrian announces his accession
n: Word of Trajan's death and his adoption reached Hadrian at Antioch.

t: Death of Hadrian
n: The emperor who crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt and refounded Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina died at Baiae.

t: Death of Antoninus Pius
n: Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus succeeded as joint emperors.

t: Death of Marcus Aurelius
n: The philosopher-emperor died on campaign on the Danube and Commodus succeeded him.

t: Commodus strangled
n: A palace conspiracy killed Commodus, opening the Year of the Five Emperors.

t: Pertinax murdered; the empire is auctioned
n: Praetorians killed Pertinax and then sold the throne to Didius Julianus.

t: Death of Septimius Severus at York
n: Severus died in Britain, leaving the empire to his sons Caracalla and Geta.

t: Geta murdered on Caracalla's orders
n: Caracalla had his brother killed, reportedly in their mother's arms.

t: Caracalla assassinated near Carrhae
n: A soldier killed Caracalla on the road to Carrhae, and the praetorian prefect Macrinus took power.

t: Death of Cao Cao
n: The warlord who had dominated northern China died at Luoyang; his son Cao Pi inherited his position.

t: Emperor Xian abdicates to Cao Pi, ending the Han
n: The last Han emperor handed over the throne, ending four centuries of Han rule and opening the Three Kingdoms era.

t: Cao Pi proclaims himself emperor of Wei
n: Cao Pi formally took the imperial title and founded the state of Cao Wei.

t: Liu Bei becomes emperor of Shu Han
n: Claiming to carry on the Han line, Liu Bei took the throne at Chengdu.

t: Death of Liu Bei at Baidicheng
n: Liu Bei died after his defeat by Wu, leaving the regency to Zhuge Liang.

t: Ardashir defeats Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan
n: Artabanus died in the battle, ending Parthian rule and beginning the Sasanian empire.

t: Sun Quan declares himself emperor of Wu
n: With this proclamation all three of the Three Kingdoms had their own emperor.

t: Death of Sun Quan
n: The founding emperor of Eastern Wu died at Jianye after a long rule.

t: Pope Sixtus II martyred in the catacombs
n: Sixtus and several deacons were executed under Valerian's edict against clergy; Lawrence followed days later.

t: Cyprian of Carthage beheaded
n: The proconsular record of the bishop's trial survives, and he was executed the same day.

t: Sima Yan proclaims the Jin dynasty
n: Four days after forcing the last Wei emperor to abdicate, Sima Yan took the throne as Emperor Wu of Jin.

t: Sun Hao surrenders, reuniting China under Jin
n: The fall of Wu ended the Three Kingdoms period.

t: Diocletian acclaimed emperor at Nicomedia
n: The army chose Diocletian after Numerian died; the Coptic Era of the Martyrs is counted from his reign.

t: Death of Emperor Wu of Jin
n: His death led to the succession of the incapable Emperor Hui and soon to the War of the Eight Princes.

t: Church at Nicomedia razed on the Terminalia
n: Diocletian chose the festival of the boundary god Terminus to begin the Great Persecution.

t: First edict of the Great Persecution published
n: The edict ordered scriptures burned, churches destroyed, and Christians stripped of legal privileges.

t: Diocletian and Maximian abdicate
n: The two senior emperors retired on the same day and handed power to Galerius and Constantius.

t: Constantius dies; Constantine acclaimed at York
n: The troops at York hailed Constantine as emperor on the day his father died.

t: Galerius' edict of toleration published
n: Lactantius says the dying Galerius' edict ending the persecution was posted at Nicomedia on the day before the Kalends of May.

t: Constantine defeats Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge
n: Constantine, who credited the Christian God with his victory, became master of the West.
s: Wikipedia: Battle of the Milvian Bridge

t: Licinius' letter on religious freedom posted at Nicomedia
n: The rescript, known as the Edict of Milan, gave back confiscated church property and granted freedom of worship.

t: Constantine defeats Licinius at Chrysopolis
n: The victory made Constantine sole emperor of the Roman world.

t: First Council of Nicaea convenes
n: Socrates gives the opening date of the first ecumenical council, which condemned Arius; some scholars put it in June.

t: Constantinople dedicated as the new capital
n: Constantine formally inaugurated his refounded city on the Bosporus.
s: OUP blog: This Day in World History

t: Annular solar eclipse recorded by Firmicus Maternus
n: The astrologer Firmicus, who later wrote a Christian polemic against paganism, mentions this eclipse in his Mathesis.
s: Wikipedia: List of solar eclipses in antiquity

t: Death of Constantine after deathbed baptism
n: Eusebius of Nicomedia baptized Constantine shortly before he died near Nicomedia.

t: Constantius II defeats Magnentius at Mursa
n: One of the bloodiest battles of the century, which badly weakened Roman manpower.

t: Death of Constantius II; Julian sole emperor
n: Constantius died marching against his rebel cousin Julian, who then openly returned to paganism.

t: Death of Julian the Apostate in Persia
n: The last pagan emperor died of a wound taken in battle during his retreat from Ctesiphon.

t: Death of Athanasius of Alexandria
n: The great defender of Nicene doctrine died in Alexandria after five exiles.

t: Ambrose consecrated bishop of Milan
n: Acclaimed bishop while still an unbaptized governor, Ambrose was baptized and consecrated within a week.

t: Death of Valentinian I
n: The emperor reportedly died of a stroke while raging at Quadi envoys.

t: Goths destroy the Roman army at Adrianople
n: Emperor Valens was killed in the worst Roman defeat in centuries.

t: Theodosius I made emperor of the East
n: Gratian raised Theodosius to rule the East after the disaster at Adrianople.

t: Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the state faith
n: Theodosius, Gratian and Valentinian II ordered all their subjects to follow the faith of the bishops of Rome and Alexandria.

t: Battle of the Frigidus begins
n: Over two days Theodosius defeated the usurper Eugenius, who was backed by the last pagan party.

t: Death of Theodosius I; empire divided
n: The last emperor to rule both halves died at Milan, leaving East to Arcadius and West to Honorius.

t: Death of Ambrose of Milan
n: The bishop who baptized Augustine and stood up to Theodosius died on Holy Saturday.

t: Death of John Chrysostom in exile
n: The deposed archbishop of Constantinople died at Comana while being moved to a harsher exile.

t: Alaric's Visigoths sack Rome
n: The Goths came in through the Salarian Gate, and the shock led Augustine to write The City of God.

t: Death of Augustine of Hippo
n: Augustine died while the Vandals were besieging Hippo.

t: Council of Ephesus opens under Cyril
n: Cyril of Alexandria opened the third ecumenical council before the Antiochene bishops arrived; it deposed Nestorius.

t: Leo the Great elected bishop of Rome
n: Leo was chosen in his absence while on a diplomatic mission in Gaul.

t: Council of Chalcedon opens
n: The fourth ecumenical council defined Christ as one person in two natures.

t: Valentinian III assassinated
n: Retainers of the murdered general Aetius killed the emperor, ending the Theodosian dynasty in the West.

t: Death of Pope Leo the Great
n: Leo, whose Tome shaped Chalcedon and who met Attila, died after 21 years as pope.

t: Total lunar eclipse recorded by Hydatius
n: The Galician bishop-chronicler recorded the eclipse in his chronicle of the barbarian invasions.

t: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus
n: The deposition of the last western emperor is traditionally taken as the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

t: Death of Julius Nepos in Dalmatia
n: Nepos was murdered in Dalmatia; he was the last western emperor still recognized by Constantinople.

t: First Code of Justinian promulgated
n: Justinian issued the first edition of his consolidated code of imperial law, which went on to underpin much of later European civil law.

t: Hagia Sophia dedicated by Justinian
n: The rebuilt Great Church of Constantinople was consecrated less than six years after the Nika riots destroyed its predecessor.

t: Second Council of Constantinople opens
n: The fifth ecumenical council met to condemn the Three Chapters and continued sitting until 2 June 553.

t: Third Council of Toledo opens; Visigoths renounce Arianism
n: King Reccared and the Visigothic nobility formally embraced Catholic Christianity at this council; some sources give 8 May for the opening.

t: Gregory the Great consecrated Bishop of Rome
n: Gregory, elected after Pelagius II died of plague, was consecrated and later sent the mission of Augustine to the English.

t: Hijra: Muhammad arrives at Quba near Medina
n: Tradition dates the arrival to Monday 8 Rabi al-Awwal; Julian conversions vary by a few days (20 to 24 September), while the Islamic era itself is counted from 16 July 622.

t: Battle of Badr
n: The Muslims of Medina defeated a larger Meccan force on 17 Ramadan AH 2; the Julian date is a calendar conversion.

t: Death of Muhammad in Medina
n: Muhammad died in Medina, and Abu Bakr was chosen as the first caliph.

t: Battle of Yarmouk ends in Arab victory
n: The decisive day of a battle lasting several days, in which Rashidun forces broke Byzantine power in Syria.

t: Battle of Karbala; Husayn ibn Ali killed
n: Husayn, grandson of Muhammad, was killed on 10 Muharram AH 61, remembered every year at Ashura.

t: Third Council of Constantinople opens
n: The sixth ecumenical council, held in the domed Trullus hall of the palace, condemned Monothelitism.

t: Battle of Tours (Poitiers)
n: Charles Martel's Franks stopped an Umayyad army; the 10 October date is traditional and some scholars prefer 733.

t: Boniface martyred at Dokkum
n: The English missionary bishop who evangelised much of Germany was killed with companions in Frisia; 5 June is his feast and traditional death day.

t: An Lushan Rebellion begins
n: An Lushan marched out of Fanyang against the Tang court, starting a war that devastated the dynasty.

t: Second Council of Nicaea opens
n: The seventh ecumenical council restored the veneration of icons, setting out its definition on 13 October.

t: Viking raid on Lindisfarne
n: Norse raiders sacked the island monastery, usually taken as the start of the Viking Age; one chronicle copy says 8 January instead.

t: Charlemagne crowned emperor in Rome
n: Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king emperor of the Romans at Christmas Mass in St Peter's.

t: Charter founding the Abbey of Cluny
n: Duke William of Aquitaine endowed a monastery free of lay control, which became the centre of a major monastic reform; some date the charter to 909.

t: Otto I crowned emperor
n: Pope John XII crowned Otto in Rome, founding what came to be called the Holy Roman Empire.

t: Battle of Clontarf
n: Brian Boru defeated Leinster and Norse forces on Good Friday but was killed in the fighting.

t: Humbert lays excommunication on Hagia Sophia altar
n: The papal legate placed a bull against Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar, the act usually taken as the start of the East-West Schism.

t: Battle of Hastings
n: William of Normandy defeated and killed King Harold II, opening the Norman Conquest.

t: William the Conqueror crowned at Westminster
n: William was crowned king on Christmas Day in Westminster Abbey.

t: Battle of Manzikert
n: The Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated and captured Emperor Romanos IV, opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

t: Henry IV absolved at Canossa
n: After standing as a penitent at the castle gate, the excommunicated king was absolved by Pope Gregory VII.

t: Urban II calls the First Crusade at Clermont
n: Pope Urban II preached in a field outside Clermont, urging Christians to go to the aid of the East and to Jerusalem.

t: First Crusade captures Jerusalem
n: Crusaders broke into the city after a siege of about five weeks and massacred many of its inhabitants.

t: Concordat of Worms
n: Emperor Henry V and Pope Callixtus II settled the Investiture Controversy over who appoints bishops.

t: Thomas Becket murdered in Canterbury Cathedral
n: Four knights of Henry II killed the archbishop in his cathedral, and he was canonised within three years.

t: Battle of Hattin
n: Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem near Tiberias, opening the way to Jerusalem.

t: Saladin takes Jerusalem
n: The city surrendered to Saladin after a short siege, ending 88 years of crusader rule.

t: Fourth Crusade storms Constantinople
n: Crusaders broke into the Christian capital and sacked it over three days, deepening the split between East and West.

t: Magna Carta sealed at Runnymede
n: King John agreed to the charter of liberties put to him by rebel barons.

t: Fourth Lateran Council opens
n: Innocent III's great council defined transubstantiation and required annual confession and communion.

t: Honorius III approves the Dominican Order
n: The bull Religiosam vitam confirmed Dominic's community of preachers at Toulouse.

t: Franciscan Rule approved by papal bull
n: Honorius III confirmed the final Rule of Francis of Assisi with the bull Solet annuere.

t: Abbasid caliph surrenders Baghdad to Hulagu
n: Caliph al-Musta'sim surrendered to the Mongols, who began sacking the city three days later.

t: Battle of Ain Jalut
n: The Mamluks of Egypt defeated a Mongol army in Galilee, halting the Mongol advance toward Egypt.

t: Boniface VIII proclaims the first Jubilee
n: The bull Antiquorum habet offered a plenary indulgence to pilgrims to Rome and began the Holy Year tradition.

t: Battle of Bannockburn
n: Robert the Bruce defeated Edward II on the second day of the battle, securing Scottish independence for a generation.

t: Declaration of Arbroath
n: Scottish nobles wrote to Pope John XXII asserting Scotland's independence and asking him to recognise Robert the Bruce as king.

t: Zhu Yuanzhang proclaims the Ming dynasty
n: At Nanjing, Zhu proclaimed himself emperor as the Hongwu Emperor, and his forces drove the Mongol Yuan from Beijing later that year.

t: Blackfriars 'Earthquake Synod' condemns Wycliffe
n: Archbishop Courtenay's council condemned Wycliffe's teachings while an earthquake shook London.

t: Jan Hus burned at Constance
n: The Czech reformer was condemned by the Council of Constance and executed despite a promise of safe conduct.

t: Battle of Agincourt
n: Henry V's outnumbered English army, relying on its longbowmen, defeated the French on St Crispin's Day.

t: Martin V elected, ending the Western Schism
n: The Council of Constance chose Oddone Colonna as the single pope, closing nearly forty years of rival papacies.

t: Joan of Arc burned at Rouen
n: After a church trial under English control, Joan was burned as a relapsed heretic; she was cleared in 1456 and canonised in 1920.

t: Council of Florence decrees union with the Greeks
n: The decree Laetentur caeli announced a reunion of the Latin and Greek churches, which was later rejected in the East.

t: Fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans
n: Mehmed II's army stormed the walls, ending the Byzantine Empire, and Hagia Sophia became a mosque.

t: Mainz Psalter completed, first dated printed book
n: Fust and Schoeffer's colophon dates the book to the eve of the Assumption and is the first to name its printers and date.

t: Kongo king Nzinga a Nkuwu baptised as Joao I
n: The king and his family received baptism from Portuguese priests, beginning Kongo's long Catholic history.

t: Granada surrenders to Ferdinand and Isabella
n: Emir Muhammad XII handed over the city, ending the last Muslim state in Iberia.

t: Alhambra Decree expels Jews from Spain
n: The Catholic Monarchs ordered all practising Jews to convert or leave their kingdoms by the end of July.

t: Columbus makes landfall in the Bahamas
n: Columbus's expedition reached an island the Lucayans called Guanahani; the date is Julian (21 October in the proleptic Gregorian).

t: Treaty of Tordesillas
n: Spain and Portugal divided newly found lands outside Europe along a meridian west of the Cape Verde islands.

t: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut
n: Da Gama's fleet arrived on the Malabar coast, opening a sea route from Europe to India around Africa.

t: Savonarola executed in Florence
n: The Dominican preacher who had dominated Florence was hanged and burned in the Piazza della Signoria.

t: Cabral's fleet sights Brazil
n: A Portuguese fleet bound for India sighted Monte Pascoal and claimed the land for Portugal.

t: Montesinos preaches against abuse of the Taino
n: On the fourth Sunday of Advent the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos denounced the colonists' treatment of the native people.

t: Complutensian Polyglot New Testament completed
n: The colophon of Cardinal Cisneros's polyglot dates the first printed Greek New Testament, though the work was not issued until about 1522.

t: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
n: Luther sent his theses against indulgences to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz; the posting on the Wittenberg church door is traditional.

t: Luther burns the papal bull Exsurge Domine
n: Outside Wittenberg's Elster Gate, Luther burned the bull threatening him with excommunication, along with books of canon law.

t: Luther refuses to recant at the Diet of Worms
n: Before Emperor Charles V, Luther declined to retract his writings unless refuted by Scripture and plain reason.

t: Fall of Tenochtitlan
n: Cuauhtemoc was captured and the Aztec capital fell to Cortes and his Tlaxcalan and other Indigenous allies after a long siege.

t: Victoria returns, completing first circumnavigation
n: Elcano brought the last ship of Magellan's expedition into Sanlucar de Barrameda with 18 survivors.

t: First believers' baptisms in Zurich
n: Conrad Grebel baptised George Blaurock at Felix Manz's house, usually taken as the founding of the Anabaptist movement.

t: First Battle of Panipat
n: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi of the Delhi Sultanate and founded the Mughal Empire.

t: Battle of Mohacs
n: Suleiman the Magnificent destroyed the Hungarian army, and King Louis II died fleeing the field.

t: Schleitheim Confession adopted
n: Swiss Brethren meeting under Michael Sattler agreed seven articles that defined early Anabaptist practice.

t: Augsburg Confession presented to Charles V
n: The Lutheran princes had Melanchthon's statement of faith read aloud at the Diet of Augsburg.

t: Our Lady of Guadalupe image revealed (tradition)
n: Catholic tradition holds that Juan Diego showed Bishop Zumarraga the image on his cloak on this day; early documentation is debated.

t: Pizarro captures Atahualpa at Cajamarca
n: Spanish forces ambushed the Inca ruler's retinue in Cajamarca's plaza and took him prisoner.

t: Coverdale Bible finished printing
n: The colophon of Myles Coverdale's translation, the first complete printed English Bible, gives 4 October 1535.

t: William Tyndale executed at Vilvoorde
n: The translator of the English New Testament was strangled and burned for heresy; 6 October is the traditional date.

t: Paul III issues Sublimis Deus
n: The bull declared that the Indigenous peoples of the Americas were rational beings who must not be enslaved or robbed.

t: Society of Jesus approved by Paul III
n: The bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae formally established Ignatius of Loyola's order.

t: Battle of Wayna Daga
n: Emperor Gelawdewos and Portuguese musketeers defeated and killed Ahmad Gran, saving the Christian Ethiopian kingdom; sources differ on the date.

t: Council of Trent opens
n: The council that framed the Catholic response to the Reformation held its first session.

t: First Book of Common Prayer comes into use
n: Cranmer's English liturgy became mandatory on Whitsunday, sparking the Prayer Book Rebellion in the West Country.

t: Francis Xavier lands at Kagoshima
n: The Jesuit missionary came ashore with Japanese convert Anjiro, beginning Christian missions in Japan.

t: Peace of Augsburg
n: The settlement let each prince of the Empire choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his own territory.

t: Scottish Parliament approves the Scots Confession
n: The Reformation Parliament adopted the Reformed confession drafted by John Knox and five colleagues.

t: Battle of Lepanto
n: The Holy League's galleys destroyed most of the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras.

t: St Bartholomew's Day massacre begins
n: Catholic mobs and royal troops in Paris killed Huguenot leaders and thousands of Protestants, and the killing spread to other cities.

t: Oda Nobunaga dies at Honno-ji
n: Akechi Mitsuhide's troops attacked the Kyoto temple and Nobunaga took his own life; this is a Julian conversion of the Japanese date (Tensho 10, 6th month, 2nd day).

t: Gregorian calendar takes effect
n: Following Gregory XIII's bull Inter gravissimas, Catholic lands went straight from Thursday 4 October to Friday 15 October.

t: Battle of Gravelines breaks the Spanish Armada
n: English fireships and guns scattered the Armada off Flanders; this is the English Old Style date, and the Spanish recorded 8 August (New Style).

t: Battle of Tondibi
n: A Moroccan army armed with firearms defeated Askia Ishaq II, bringing about the collapse of the Songhai Empire.

t: Edict of Nantes
n: Henry IV gave French Protestants legal toleration and civil rights, ending the Wars of Religion.

t: Battle of Sekigahara
n: Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory led to the Tokugawa shogunate; this is a conversion of the Japanese date (Keicho 5, 9th month, 15th day).

t: Matteo Ricci enters Beijing
n: The Jesuit missionary arrived at the Ming capital and was later allowed to stay there under the Wanli Emperor's patronage.

t: English colonists land at Jamestown
n: The Virginia Company settlers came ashore on the James River and built James Fort; the date is Old Style (24 May New Style).

t: Champlain founds Quebec
n: Samuel de Champlain set up his habitation at the narrows of the St Lawrence, the start of Quebec City.

t: Defenestration of Prague
n: Protestant nobles threw two Catholic imperial regents and their secretary from a window of Prague Castle, triggering the Thirty Years' War.

t: Synod of Dort opens
n: The international Reformed synod at Dordrecht answered the Remonstrants and produced the Canons of Dort, closing on 9 May 1619.

t: Mayflower Compact signed
n: At anchor off Cape Cod, the Pilgrims and other passengers agreed to form a civil body politic; the date is Old Style (21 November New Style).

t: Ville-Marie (Montreal) founded
n: Maisonneuve and about fifty settlers founded a missionary colony on the island of Montreal.

t: Peace of Westphalia signed
n: The treaties of Munster and Osnabruck ended the Thirty Years' War and recognised Calvinism alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism in the Empire.

t: Execution of Charles I
n: The king was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall; contemporaries wrote 1648 because their year began on 25 March, and the New Style date is 9 February.

t: Pascal's 'night of fire'
n: Blaise Pascal recorded an intense religious experience on a parchment he kept sewn into his coat until he died.

t: The Great Ejection
n: About two thousand ministers who would not conform to the Act of Uniformity lost their livings on St Bartholomew's Day (3 September New Style).

t: Battle of Mbwila
n: Portuguese forces from Luanda defeated and killed King Antonio I of Kongo, setting off decades of civil war in the kingdom.

t: Great Fire of London begins
n: A fire in a bakery on Pudding Lane burned for four days and destroyed most of the medieval City, including old St Paul's (12 September New Style).

t: Edict of Fontainebleau revokes Nantes
n: Louis XIV outlawed Protestant worship, and roughly 200,000 Huguenots fled abroad.

t: William of Orange lands at Torbay
n: William's landing at Brixham began the Glorious Revolution that removed James II; the date is Old Style (15 November New Style).

t: Toleration Act receives royal assent
n: The Act allowed Protestant dissenters who took certain oaths to worship freely in licensed meeting houses (3 June New Style).

t: Battle of the Boyne
n: William III defeated James II near Drogheda; the date is Old Style (11 July New Style), and the battle is now marked on 12 July.

t: Peter the Great founds Saint Petersburg
n: Work began on the Peter and Paul Fortress on Hare Island in the Neva; Russia used the Julian calendar, and the New Style date is 27 May.

t: Ziegenbalg and Plutschau land at Tranquebar
n: The first Protestant missionaries to India arrived at the Danish colony, and Ziegenbalg later translated the New Testament into Tamil.

t: Moravian refugees found Herrnhut
n: Christian David felled the first tree for a settlement on Count Zinzendorf's estate, which became the centre of the renewed Moravian Church.

t: Moravian 'Pentecost' at Berthelsdorf
n: A communion service brought renewal and reconciliation to the Herrnhut community, followed by a century-long round-the-clock prayer watch.

t: First Moravian missionaries reach St Thomas
n: Leonhard Dober and David Nitschmann arrived in the Danish West Indies to preach to enslaved Africans.

t: John Wesley's Aldersgate experience
n: Listening to Luther's preface to Romans read aloud, Wesley felt his heart 'strangely warmed' (4 June New Style).

t: Whitefield's first open-air sermon at Kingswood
n: Whitefield preached in the open air to coal miners near Bristol, a key step in the field preaching of the Evangelical Revival; contemporaries wrote 1738/9 (28 February New Style).

t: Edwards preaches 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God'
n: Jonathan Edwards's sermon at Enfield became the best-known sermon of the Great Awakening (19 July New Style).

t: Premiere of Handel's Messiah in Dublin
n: The oratorio was first performed at the New Music Hall in Fishamble Street as a charity benefit (24 April New Style).

t: Battle of Culloden
n: Government forces crushed Charles Edward Stuart's Jacobite army near Inverness (27 April New Style).

t: Halifax founded by Edward Cornwallis
n: Cornwallis arrived at Chebucto with settlers to found Halifax, on land the Mi'kmaq had not ceded; this is the Old Style date (2 July New Style).

t: Britain and its colonies adopt the Gregorian calendar
n: Under the Calendar Act, Wednesday 2 September was followed by Thursday 14 September, and the legal year already began on 1 January.

t: Expulsion order read to the Acadians at Grand-Pre
n: Lt Col John Winslow read the deportation order to Acadian men gathered in the Grand-Pre church.

t: Great Lisbon earthquake
n: On All Saints' morning an earthquake, tsunami and fires destroyed most of Lisbon and shook European theology and philosophy.

t: Battle of Plassey
n: Robert Clive's East India Company forces defeated Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah, starting British rule in Bengal.

t: Battle of the Plains of Abraham
n: Wolfe's British army defeated Montcalm's outside Quebec, and both generals were mortally wounded.

t: Fall of Ayutthaya
n: Burmese forces breached the walls after a 14-month siege and destroyed the Siamese capital.

t: Boston Tea Party
n: Colonists protesting the Tea Act dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into Boston Harbor.

t: Battles of Lexington and Concord
n: Fighting between British regulars and colonial militia began the American Revolutionary War.

t: Declaration of Independence adopted
n: The Continental Congress in Philadelphia approved the final text declaring the thirteen colonies independent.

t: Christmas Conference founds American Methodism
n: Preachers meeting at Lovely Lane Chapel in Baltimore organised the Methodist Episcopal Church and chose Asbury and Coke as superintendents.

t: First Fleet at Sydney Cove
n: Arthur Phillip raised the British flag at Sydney Cove, founding the convict colony of New South Wales on Aboriginal land.

t: George Washington inaugurated
n: Washington took the oath as the first President of the United States at Federal Hall.

t: Storming of the Bastille
n: A Paris crowd seized the royal fortress-prison, a defining moment of the French Revolution.

t: Bois Caiman ceremony
n: A nighttime gathering of enslaved people led by Dutty Boukman preceded the uprising that began the Haitian Revolution; the exact date rests on later accounts.

t: Baptist Missionary Society founded at Kettering
n: Twelve Baptist ministers, urged on by William Carey, formed the society in Widow Wallis's parlour, launching the modern missionary movement.

t: Execution of Louis XVI
n: The deposed king was guillotined in the Place de la Revolution after the Convention convicted him of treason.

t: William Carey arrives in Bengal
n: Carey and John Thomas reached Calcutta on a Danish ship after five months at sea; some accounts give 12 November.

t: Church Missionary Society founded
n: Evangelical Anglicans of the Clapham circle formed the society at the Castle and Falcon inn in London to send missionaries to Africa and the East.

t: Rosetta Stone discovered
n: French soldiers found the stele at Rashid, and its parallel texts later allowed hieroglyphs to be deciphered; accounts differ between 15 and 19 July.

t: Serampore Mission established by Carey, Marshman and Ward
n: William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward set up the Baptist mission at Danish Serampore, which went on to translate and print the Bible in many Indian languages.

t: British and Foreign Bible Society founded
n: The society was formed at the London Tavern to distribute the Scriptures without note or comment, becoming a model for Bible societies worldwide.

t: Battle of Trafalgar
n: A British fleet under Nelson defeated the combined French and Spanish fleets off Cape Trafalgar; Nelson was killed in the action.

t: Adoniram and Ann Judson sail from Salem for Asia
n: Among the first American overseas missionaries, the Judsons left Salem on the brig Caravan; they later served for decades in Burma.

t: Battle of Borodino
n: Napoleon's army and the Russian army under Kutuzov fought the bloodiest single day of the 1812 campaign west of Moscow (26 August Old Style).

t: Battle of Waterloo
n: Allied forces under Wellington and Prussian troops under Blücher defeated Napoleon, ending his final return to power.

t: American Bible Society founded
n: Delegates from local Bible societies met in New York City and formed a national society to publish and distribute the Bible.

t: Stockton and Darlington Railway opens
n: The line opened with George Stephenson's Locomotion No. 1 hauling the first train, the first public railway to use steam locomotives.

t: Slavery Abolition Act takes effect
n: The British act abolishing slavery in most of the Empire, including British North America, came into force.

t: Morse sends "What hath God wrought"
n: Samuel Morse sent the first official long-distance telegraph message from Washington to Baltimore, quoting Numbers 23:23.

t: YMCA founded in London
n: George Williams and fellow drapery workers founded the Young Men's Christian Association for prayer and Bible study.

t: Nova Scotia gains responsible government
n: A new Executive Council answerable to the elected assembly was sworn in, the first responsible government in what is now Canada.

t: Hudson Taylor sails for China
n: James Hudson Taylor left Liverpool aboard the Dumfries on his first voyage to China as a missionary.

t: First Fulton Street noon prayer meeting
n: Jeremiah Lanphier's lunchtime prayer meeting in New York grew into the widespread Prayer Meeting Revival of 1857-58.

t: Tischendorf is shown Codex Sinaiticus
n: On his third visit to St Catherine's Monastery, Constantin von Tischendorf was shown the bulk of the fourth-century Bible manuscript.

t: Darwin's On the Origin of Species published
n: Charles Darwin's book setting out the theory of evolution by natural selection was published in London.

t: Russia's Emancipation Manifesto frees the serfs
n: Tsar Alexander II signed the manifesto and statutes abolishing serfdom (19 February Old Style).

t: Bombardment of Fort Sumter opens the US Civil War
n: Confederate batteries fired on the federal fort in Charleston Harbor, beginning the American Civil War.

t: Charlottetown Conference opens
n: Delegates from the Maritimes and the Province of Canada met to discuss union, a first step toward Confederation.

t: Lee surrenders at Appomattox Court House
n: General Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Ulysses S. Grant, effectively ending the Civil War.

t: William Booth begins the East London mission
n: Booth's tent meetings in Whitechapel began the Christian Mission, renamed the Salvation Army in 1878.

t: Lammermuir Party sails for China
n: Hudson Taylor and the first large group of China Inland Mission workers sailed from London on the clipper Lammermuir.

t: Canadian Confederation
n: The British North America Act took effect, uniting Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and the Province of Canada as the Dominion of Canada.

t: Golden Spike completes US transcontinental railroad
n: The Central Pacific and Union Pacific lines were joined at Promontory Summit, Utah.

t: Suez Canal opens
n: The canal linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea was formally opened to shipping.

t: Vatican I defines papal infallibility
n: The First Vatican Council approved the constitution Pastor aeternus on papal primacy and infallibility.

t: Wreck of the SS Atlantic off Nova Scotia
n: The White Star liner struck rocks near Terence Bay in the early hours, with heavy loss of life; local residents rescued many survivors.

t: Bell makes the first telephone call
n: Alexander Graham Bell spoke to his assistant Thomas Watson over his new instrument in Boston.

t: Climactic eruption of Krakatoa
n: A series of colossal explosions destroyed most of the volcanic island and generated deadly tsunamis.

t: Ginsburg declares the Shapira Deuteronomy strips a forgery
n: Christian David Ginsburg of the British Museum published his judgment that the leather strips Moses Shapira said came from near the Dead Sea were fake, a verdict some scholars now question in light of Qumran.

t: Moses Shapira dies in Rotterdam
n: Disgraced after his scroll was rejected, the Jerusalem antiquities dealer took his own life in a Rotterdam hotel; the strips later vanished after an 1885 sale.

t: Last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway
n: Donald Smith drove the last spike at Craigellachie, completing Canada's first transcontinental railway.

t: First Zionist Congress opens in Basel
n: Theodor Herzl convened the congress that adopted the Basel Program calling for a Jewish home in the Land of Israel.

t: Gideons organized in Janesville
n: Three Christian commercial travelers formally organized the association later known for placing Bibles in hotels.

t: Agnes Ozman speaks in tongues at Topeka
n: At Charles Parham's Bethel Bible College, Ozman's experience became a starting point of modern Pentecostalism.

t: Marconi receives first transatlantic radio signal
n: At Signal Hill, St. John's, Marconi reported hearing the Morse letter S sent from Poldhu, Cornwall.

t: Wright brothers' first powered flight
n: Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first controlled, sustained powered airplane flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.

t: Evan Roberts' first revival meeting at Loughor
n: A small meeting of young people at Moriah chapel is generally regarded as the start of the 1904-05 Welsh Revival.

t: Bloody Sunday in St Petersburg
n: Troops fired on a peaceful procession of workers petitioning the tsar, sparking the 1905 Revolution (9 January Old Style).

t: Revival begins at Bonnie Brae Street, Los Angeles
n: Prayer meetings led by William J. Seymour broke out in tongues and soon moved to 312 Azusa Street, launching the Azusa Street Revival.

t: San Francisco earthquake
n: A major earthquake and the fires that followed destroyed much of San Francisco.

t: Silver Dart makes Canada's first powered flight
n: J.A.D. McCurdy flew the Aerial Experiment Association's Silver Dart over the ice of Bras d'Or Lake at Baddeck.

t: World Missionary Conference opens in Edinburgh
n: The gathering of Protestant mission societies is often seen as the starting point of the modern ecumenical movement.

t: RMS Titanic sinks
n: The liner sank after striking an iceberg; many of the recovered victims were brought to Halifax and buried there.

t: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
n: Gavrilo Princip shot the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne in Sarajevo, setting off the crisis that led to the First World War.

t: Britain declares war on Germany
n: Britain's declaration brought Canada and the rest of the Empire into the First World War.

t: Tsar Nicholas II abdicates
n: During the February Revolution the tsar signed his abdication at Pskov, ending Romanov rule (2 March Old Style).

t: Battle of Vimy Ridge begins
n: All four divisions of the Canadian Corps attacked together and captured the ridge over the following days.

t: Balfour Declaration
n: Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour's letter to Lord Rothschild stated British support for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine.

t: October Revolution in Petrograd
n: The Bolsheviks seized power from the Provisional Government; the Winter Palace fell overnight (25 October Old Style).

t: Halifax Explosion
n: The munitions ship Mont-Blanc collided with the Imo in the Narrows and exploded, killing about 2,000 people and devastating north-end Halifax.

t: General Allenby enters Jerusalem
n: The British commander entered the Old City on foot through the Jaffa Gate after Ottoman forces withdrew.

t: Armistice ends fighting in the First World War
n: The armistice signed at Compiègne took effect at 11 a.m., ending hostilities on the Western Front.

t: Treaty of Versailles signed
n: The peace treaty between Germany and the Allied powers was signed in the Hall of Mirrors.

t: Schooner Bluenose launched at Lunenburg
n: The fishing and racing schooner built by Smith and Rhuland went on to become an emblem of Nova Scotia.

t: United Church of Canada inaugurated
n: Methodists, Congregationalists and most Presbyterians united at a service in Toronto's Mutual Street Arena.

t: Pier 21 opens in Halifax
n: The ocean immigration shed opened; about a million immigrants, refugees and war brides later entered Canada through it.

t: Black Tuesday stock market crash
n: Panic selling on the New York Stock Exchange marked the deepest day of the 1929 crash and the onset of the Great Depression.

t: Barmen Theological Declaration adopted
n: The Confessing Synod at Barmen affirmed the sole lordship of Christ over the church against state-imposed ideology.

t: Kristallnacht pogrom
n: Over the night of 9-10 November, synagogues, Jewish homes and businesses across Germany and Austria were attacked.

t: Germany invades Poland
n: The German invasion began the Second World War in Europe.

t: Canada declares war on Germany
n: In its first independent declaration of war, Canada entered the Second World War a week after Britain.

t: Attack on Pearl Harbor
n: Japanese aircraft attacked the US Pacific Fleet in Hawaii, bringing the United States into the war.

t: Wannsee Conference
n: Senior Nazi officials met near Berlin to coordinate the deportation and murder of Europe's Jews.

t: D-Day landings in Normandy
n: Allied forces, including Canadians at Juno Beach, landed in Normandy to open a western front.

t: Liberation of Auschwitz
n: Soviet troops reached the Auschwitz camp complex; the date is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

t: Dietrich Bonhoeffer executed
n: The Lutheran pastor and theologian, an opponent of the Nazi regime, was hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp.

t: Victory in Europe Day
n: The Allies formally accepted Germany's unconditional surrender, ending the war in Europe.

t: Atomic bombing of Hiroshima
n: A US aircraft dropped the first atomic bomb used in war on Hiroshima.

t: United Nations Charter enters into force
n: The UN came into existence once the Charter had been ratified by the required states; the date is marked as UN Day.

t: Viola Desmond refuses to leave a whites-only section
n: The Halifax businesswoman was arrested at New Glasgow's Roseland Theatre, a landmark in Canadian civil rights history.

t: India and Pakistan become independent
n: British rule ended and India became independent, a day after Pakistan's creation, amid the partition of the subcontinent.

t: UN adopts the Partition Plan for Palestine
n: General Assembly Resolution 181 recommended dividing Mandatory Palestine into Jewish and Arab states with an international Jerusalem.

t: Sukenik buys the first scrolls in Bethlehem
n: Eleazar Sukenik of the Hebrew University crossed to Bethlehem and bought Cave 1 scrolls for the Jewish people on the very day the UN voted to partition Palestine.

t: Sukenik acquires another Cave 1 scroll
n: Less than a month after his first purchase, Sukenik obtained a further scroll from the same Bethlehem source, completing the Hebrew University's set of three.
s: Schiffman, Reclaiming the Dead Sea Scrolls

t: John Trever photographs the scrolls at ASOR
n: At the American School of Oriental Research, John Trever photographed the Great Isaiah Scroll, the Community Rule and the Habakkuk Commentary brought from St Mark's Monastery. He worked with them over roughly 18 to 21 February; 21 February is the date usually given.

t: Albright hails the greatest manuscript find of modern times
n: After seeing Trever's prints, William F. Albright wrote back congratulating him on what he called the greatest manuscript discovery of modern times. The original letter is dated 8 March 1948.

t: ASOR and Yale announce the discovery to the world
n: Millar Burrows of ASOR issued the press release, through Yale, that first made the scrolls public news. Most sources give 11 April; John J. Collins dates the Yale News Bureau release to 10 April.
s: Wikipedia; Collins, The Dead Sea Scrolls: A Biography

t: Sukenik announces the Hebrew University scrolls
n: Two weeks after the American announcement, Sukenik issued his own statement about the scrolls he had bought for the Hebrew University.

t: Israel's Declaration of Independence
n: David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel in Tel Aviv as the British Mandate ended.

t: World Council of Churches founded
n: The WCC was formally constituted at its first assembly in Amsterdam.

t: Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted
n: The UN General Assembly in Paris adopted the declaration, drafted with Canadian John Humphrey's involvement.

t: Cave 1 located by Lippens and el-Zebn
n: Belgian UN observer Captain Philippe Lippens and Arab Legion Captain Akkash el-Zebn found the cave where the first scrolls had been discovered.

t: Mar Samuel takes four scrolls to the United States
n: The Syrian Metropolitan Athanasius Yeshue Samuel left for America with his four Cave 1 scrolls to exhibit them and find a buyer. Sources agree on January 1949; the day comes from a single chronology.

t: Harding and de Vaux begin excavating Cave 1
n: The Jordanian Department of Antiquities and the Ecole Biblique, led by G. Lankester Harding and Roland de Vaux, dug Cave 1 from 15 February to 5 March, recovering fragments and pottery.

t: Newfoundland joins Canada
n: Newfoundland became Canada's tenth province just before midnight on 31 March.

t: Billy Graham's Los Angeles campaign begins
n: The eight-week tent campaign brought Graham to national prominence.

t: First US exhibition of the scrolls opens at the Library of Congress
n: Three of Mar Samuel's scrolls went on show at the Library of Congress, opening to invited guests and to the public the next day.

t: Libby radiocarbon-dates Cave 1 linen
n: Willard Libby tested linen wrapping from Cave 1 in one of the earliest archaeological uses of radiocarbon dating, placing it around the turn of the era.
s: Wikipedia: Carbon dating the Dead Sea Scrolls

t: First excavation season at Khirbet Qumran
n: De Vaux and Harding began digging the ruins beside the caves, a season that ran to 12 December and linked the settlement to the scroll jars.
s: Schiffman, Reclaiming the Dead Sea Scrolls

t: Copper Scroll found in Cave 3
n: An ASOR and Ecole Biblique survey entered Cave 3 and found two rolled copper sheets listing hidden treasure, along with other fragments.

t: Cave 4 excavated by Harding, de Vaux and Milik
n: After Bedouin looted the richest cave of all, archaeologists excavated Cave 4 from 22 to 29 September, recovering part of a trove of some 15,000 fragments.

t: Eleazar Sukenik dies
n: The archaeologist who first recognized the scrolls' age and bought three of them died in Jerusalem, before his son could bring the rest to Israel.

t: Scrolls advertised for sale in the Wall Street Journal
n: A classified notice headed "The Four Dead Sea Scrolls" offered Mar Samuel's manuscripts for sale; Yigael Yadin, then in the US, learned of it and arranged a secret purchase.

t: Four scrolls bought for Israel at the Waldorf-Astoria
n: The scrolls were handed over at the Waldorf-Astoria and bought through intermediaries for $250,000 on behalf of Yadin and the State of Israel.

t: Israel announces it owns the four Samuel scrolls
n: Prime Minister Moshe Sharett revealed the purchase, reuniting all seven original Cave 1 scrolls in Israel, and proposed a special building to house them.

t: Five missionaries killed in Ecuador
n: Jim Elliot, Nate Saint and three colleagues were killed by Waorani men; family members later lived among the Waorani.

t: Sputnik 1 launched
n: The Soviet Union put the first artificial satellite into orbit.

t: Springhill mining disaster
n: An underground 'bump' in the Springhill coal mine killed 75 miners; others were rescued after days underground.

t: Adolf Eichmann captured in Buenos Aires
n: Israeli agents seized the Holocaust organizer, who was later tried and executed in Israel.

t: Yuri Gagarin becomes the first human in space
n: Gagarin orbited Earth once aboard Vostok 1.

t: Construction of the Berlin Wall begins
n: East German authorities sealed the border between East and West Berlin overnight.

t: Second Vatican Council opens
n: Pope John XXIII opened the council that reshaped Catholic liturgy and relations with other churches.

t: President John F. Kennedy assassinated
n: Kennedy was shot and killed in a motorcade in Dallas, Texas.

t: Maple Leaf flag first raised
n: The new National Flag of Canada was officially inaugurated on Parliament Hill.

t: Shrine of the Book opens
n: The Israel Museum's white-domed shrine, shaped after the lids of the scroll jars, opened to house the Cave 1 scrolls.

t: Israeli paratroopers reach the Temple Mount
n: During the Six-Day War, Israeli forces took the Old City; commander Motta Gur radioed "The Temple Mount is in our hands."

t: Temple Scroll recovered from Kando
n: During the Six-Day War, officers sent by Yigael Yadin went with the dealer Kando to Bethlehem on the evening of 8 June and recovered the longest Qumran scroll, hidden under his floor.
s: Silberman, A Prophet from Amongst You

t: Apollo 11 lands on the Moon
n: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first humans to land on the Moon.

t: Roland de Vaux dies
n: The Dominican scholar who excavated Qumran and led the official scroll team died with his final excavation report still unpublished.

t: Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization opens
n: Some 2,700 evangelical leaders gathered and produced the Lausanne Covenant.

t: Entebbe raid
n: Israeli commandos rescued hostages from a hijacked airliner at Entebbe airport.

t: Camp David Accords signed
n: Egypt's Sadat and Israel's Begin signed frameworks for peace brokered by Jimmy Carter.

t: Constitution Act, 1982 proclaimed
n: Queen Elizabeth II proclaimed the patriated constitution, including the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, in Ottawa.

t: Yigael Yadin dies
n: The soldier and archaeologist who secured four Cave 1 scrolls and the Temple Scroll for Israel died aged 67.

t: Chernobyl nuclear disaster
n: Reactor No. 4 at the Chernobyl plant exploded, releasing radioactive material across Europe.

t: Fall of the Berlin Wall
n: East Germany opened its border crossings, and crowds began crossing and dismantling the Wall.

t: Operation Solomon airlifts Ethiopian Jews
n: In about 36 hours over 24-25 May, Israel flew some 14,000 Ethiopian Jews from Addis Ababa to Israel.

t: Computer-reconstructed scroll texts unveiled
n: Ben Zion Wacholder and Martin Abegg announced texts rebuilt by computer from the official team's concordance, published by the Biblical Archaeology Society, breaking the monopoly on unpublished Cave 4 material.

t: Huntington Library opens its scroll photographs to all
n: The Huntington announced it would let any qualified scholar consult its full set of master photographs of the scrolls, effectively ending restricted access.

t: BAS releases the facsimile edition of unpublished scrolls
n: The Biblical Archaeology Society published nearly 1,800 photographs of unpublished fragments in two volumes edited by Eisenman and Robinson.

t: Soviet Union formally dissolved
n: The Supreme Soviet's upper chamber voted the USSR out of existence, a day after Gorbachev resigned.

t: Westray Mine explosion
n: A methane and coal-dust explosion at Plymouth, Pictou County, killed all 26 miners underground.

t: Jerusalem court rules for Qimron over the MMT text
n: Judge Dalia Dorner held that Elisha Qimron owned the copyright in his reconstruction of the Halakhic Letter (4QMMT), which BAS had printed without permission. News reports appeared on 31 March.

t: Oslo I Accord signed
n: Israel and the PLO signed the Declaration of Principles at the White House.

t: Toronto Airport Vineyard revival begins
n: Meetings with Randy Clark began a long-running charismatic revival known as the Toronto Blessing.

t: Nelson Mandela inaugurated president
n: Mandela became South Africa's first president elected in a fully representative democratic election.

t: Swissair Flight 111 crashes off Peggy's Cove
n: The MD-11 crashed into St. Margarets Bay after an in-flight fire, killing all 229 aboard.

t: Catholic-Lutheran Joint Declaration on Justification
n: The Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed a common statement on justification in Augsburg.

t: Israel's Supreme Court upholds Qimron's copyright
n: A panel led by Aharon Barak upheld the 1993 verdict that a scholar's reconstruction of a scroll text is protected work. Reported in the New York Times on 31 August.

t: September 11 attacks
n: Hijacked airliners struck the World Trade Center and Pentagon; diverted flights landed in Gander and Halifax.

t: Hurricane Juan strikes Halifax
n: Juan made landfall near Halifax as a Category 2 hurricane, causing deaths and widespread damage.

t: Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami
n: A magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra generated tsunamis that killed about 230,000 people in many countries.

t: Pope John Paul II dies
n: The Polish-born pope died after a pontificate of more than 26 years.

t: Apple announces the iPhone
n: Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone, which helped define the smartphone era.

t: Tohoku earthquake, tsunami and Fukushima accident
n: A magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami killed nearly 20,000 people and triggered the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident.

t: Israel Museum and Google put five scrolls online
n: High-resolution, searchable images of the Great Isaiah Scroll and four other Cave 1 scrolls went live. Wikipedia gives 25 September; contemporary reports say 26 September.

t: CERN announces Higgs boson discovery
n: The ATLAS and CMS experiments reported observing a new particle consistent with the Higgs boson.

t: Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library launches
n: The Israel Antiquities Authority, with Google, launched its online library of thousands of fragment images in colour and infrared.

t: Pope Benedict XVI's resignation takes effect
n: Benedict became the first pope in nearly six centuries to resign.

t: En-Gedi Leviticus scroll read by virtual unwrapping
n: A team led by Brent Seales published scans revealing Leviticus text inside a charred scroll from En-Gedi, the oldest Pentateuch scroll found since Qumran.

t: Twelfth Qumran scroll cave announced
n: Hebrew University and Israel Antiquities Authority archaeologists reported a cave that once held scrolls, with jars, wrappings, a blank parchment and pickaxes left by looters.

t: Museum of the Bible says five fragments are forgeries
n: Tests by Germany's Federal Institute for Materials Research led the museum to withdraw five of its sixteen "Dead Sea Scroll" fragments as probable modern fakes.

t: WHO declares COVID-19 a pandemic
n: The World Health Organization characterized the COVID-19 outbreak as a pandemic.

t: All sixteen Museum of the Bible fragments found to be fake
n: An independent investigation presented at a museum conference concluded that every one of its sixteen fragments was a modern forgery on ancient leather.

t: Abraham Accords signed
n: Israel, the UAE and Bahrain signed normalization agreements at the White House.

t: IAA unveils new scroll fragments from the Cave of Horror
n: The Israel Antiquities Authority presented about 80 new pieces of a Greek Minor Prophets scroll, the first new biblical scroll fragments found in excavation in some 60 years.

t: James Webb Space Telescope launched
n: An Ariane 5 rocket launched the telescope, built by NASA with ESA and the Canadian Space Agency.

t: Russia launches full-scale invasion of Ukraine
n: Russian forces invaded Ukraine on several fronts, beginning Europe's largest war since 1945.

t: Queen Elizabeth II dies
n: The Queen of the United Kingdom and Canada died at Balmoral after a 70-year reign; Charles III succeeded her.

t: Post-tropical storm Fiona hits Nova Scotia
n: Fiona made landfall in eastern Nova Scotia, causing record low pressure and severe damage across Atlantic Canada.

t: Asbury revival begins
n: A routine chapel service at Asbury University in Kentucky continued for about two weeks of round-the-clock worship.

t: Hamas-led attack on Israel
n: Militants from Gaza killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel and took some 250 hostages, starting the Gaza war.

t: Notre-Dame de Paris reopens
n: The cathedral reopened with a ceremony five years after the 2019 fire.

t: Fall of the Assad government in Syria
n: Opposition forces entered Damascus and Bashar al-Assad fled the country.

t: Mark Carney sworn in as prime minister
n: Carney succeeded Justin Trudeau as Canada's 24th prime minister.

t: Pope Francis dies
n: The first Latin American pope died on Easter Monday at age 88.

t: Pope Leo XIV elected
n: Cardinal Robert Prevost was elected as the first pope from the United States.

t: Enoch AI study redates many scrolls earlier
n: Mladen Popovic's team combined new radiocarbon tests with machine-learning handwriting analysis, concluding that many scrolls are older than thought and two biblical fragments come from their books' traditional era.

t: Israel strikes Iran, beginning a twelve-day war
n: Israel attacked Iranian nuclear and military sites; a ceasefire took effect on 24 June.

t: Last living Israeli hostages released from Gaza
n: Under a ceasefire deal, Hamas freed the remaining 20 living hostages and Israel released Palestinian prisoners.

t: US strikes Venezuela and captures Maduro
n: US forces carried out strikes in Venezuela and took Nicolás Maduro into custody to face charges in New York.

t: Milano Cortina Winter Olympics open
n: The XXV Olympic Winter Games opened with a ceremony at Milan's San Siro stadium.

t: Ayatollah Khamenei killed in US-Israeli strikes
n: Iran's supreme leader was killed in strikes on the first day of a US-Israeli military campaign against Iran.

t: Artemis II launches crew around the Moon
n: NASA launched four astronauts, including Canadian Jeremy Hansen, on the first crewed lunar mission since 1972; they splashed down on 10 April.

t: Twin earthquakes strike Venezuela
n: Two major earthquakes caused thousands of deaths and widespread destruction.

t: Spain wins the 2026 FIFA World Cup
n: Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in the final of the first World Cup co-hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States.

t: Year 6000 AM begins
n: Close of the 12th Onah and the Age of Grace in this calendar's scheme.
b: Ken Johnson's stated year

t: First year of the Age of the Kingdom (6001 AM)
n: Start of the 13th Onah in this calendar's scheme.
b: Ken Johnson's stated year
